title: The ancient origins of Sci-fi and tech words

entries.note: In Greek a discourse or treatise on the arts, from a root meaning to weave or fabricate; by the 1700s it meant mechanical and industrial arts.
Interneted meant interwoven in the 1800s; the tech sense dates from 1945 as US War Department shorthand for inter-network, and the capital I was dropped by 2016.
A system shaped physically or figuratively like a net, dating back to the 1500s, when spiderwebs and artistic elements were described as networks.
With intra meaning within, it is more etymologically pure than [[see:internet]], which is a contraction of inter-network rather than meaning across networks.
Like [[see:internet]], originally written with a capital letter that has since been dropped.
British word for a vacuum cleaner, named after a specific brand, which gains ubiquity but loses credit when rivals' products are also called Hoovers.
Term for a brand name becoming the generic word for a thing, as happened with [[see:Hoover]], [[see:zipper]] and [[see:Jacuzzi]].
An example of [[see:trademark death]], a brand name turned generic word.
Perhaps not yet a victim of [[see:trademark death]], the hosts suggest.
An example of [[see:trademark death]], a brand name turned generic word.
An example of [[see:trademark death]], a brand name turned generic word.
An example of [[see:trademark death]], a brand name turned generic word.
An example of [[see:trademark death]], a brand name turned generic word.
Plural of datum, a thing given, matching French [[equivalent:données]]; now used as singular, despite complaints in Nature as early as 1949.
The French word for data, literally things given, which matches the etymology of [[equivalent:data]]; related to [[same-root:donner (French)]].
Related to [[same-root:data]]; it just means a given time.
Named as related to [[same-root:data]].
Named as related to [[same-root:data]].
Named as related to [[same-root:data]] and to the French verb [[same-root:donner (French)]].
The French verb to give, related to [[same-root:donor]] and [[same-root:données]].
Its misuse is a complaint that seems modern but predates the complainers, like grumbling over singular [[see:data]]; Jane Austen's novels joke about it.
Jane Austen's novels contain jokes about people misusing figuratively and [[see:literally]].
One of the familiar units in the ascending scale of data volumes, before [[see:terabyte]].
A familiar unit of data volume, between [[see:gigabyte]] and [[see:petabyte]].
A unit of data volume that some people know about, below the [[see:exabyte]].
A thousand [[see:petabyte]]s, the next unit after peta.
A thousand [[see:exabyte]]s, using the prefix [[from:zetta]].
A thousand [[see:zettabyte]]s, using the prefix [[from:yotta]].
Originally eight [[see:bit]]s.
Chosen as a sort of portmanteau of binary digit.
Prefix for 10^21 accepted in the 1990s, a deliberate distortion of Latin [[from:septem]], with Z avoiding confusion with S for seconds; unrelated to Greek [[unrelated:zeta]].
Prefix for 10^24 accepted in the 1990s, a deliberate distortion of Latin [[from:octo]].
The Greek letter, which the hosts note is not the source of [[unrelated:zetta]].
Prefix for 10^-21, the small counterpart of [[see:zetta]].
Prefix for 10^-24, the small counterpart of [[see:yotta]].
Taken from [[from:cybernetics]]; tacked onto almost anything in the 1990s to suggest the internet, it now sounds old-fashioned.
From Greek [[from:kybernetes]], steersman, implying governing; [[gave:cyber]] by rebracketing, perhaps through folk association with net, and partly inspired by Ampère's [[from?:cybernétique]].
[[see:André-Marie Ampère]]'s name for the future science of government, the study of governing things, a likely partial inspiration for [[gave?:cybernetics]].
French physicist and mathematician who coined [[see:cybernétique]] and whose name inspired [[gave:amp]]s and [[gave:amperage]].
Named after [[from:André-Marie Ampère]].
Named after [[from:André-Marie Ampère]].
A 1990s coinage showing [[from:cyber]] attached to anything.
A 1990s coinage with [[from:cyber]], which would now sound cringy.
An example of [[from:cyber]] being added to other words.
An example of [[from:cyber]] being added to other words.
Contraction of cybernetic organism, first cited in the New York Times in 1960 about modifying humans to survive in space; it [[gave:Borg]].
Formed by rebracketing [[from:cyborg]].
Means slave in Czech; entered English in a 1923 translation of [[see:R.U.R.]], coined by [[see:Josef Čapek]], from [[from:robotnik]].
[[see:Karel Čapek]]'s 1920 Czech play, standing for Rossum's Universal Robots, which introduced [[see:robot]]; its robots are organic androids.
Means forced worker, originally from an Old Slavonic word for slave; source of [[gave:robot]].
Its connection with Slavonic was addressed in an earlier episode.
Author of [[see:R.U.R.]], who originally wanted to call his robots [[see:labori]].
[[see:Karel Čapek]]'s brother, who came up with the term [[see:robot]].
The earlier word for robots, broader in meaning: any supposedly self-operating machine, associated with Greek mythology and the [[see:Mechanical Turk]].
Also called the Turk, a supposedly autonomous chess-playing [[see:automaton]] first displayed in 1770, though apparently it wasn't.
[[see:Karel Čapek]]'s original name for his robots, from the Latin for work, before [[see:robot]] was chosen.
Created by rebracketing [[from:android]].
Meaning man-shaped, first used by [[see:Gabriel Naudé]] in the 1600s to dismiss [[see:Albertus Magnus]]'s supposed metal talking head; it [[gave:droid]].
Louis XIII's personal doctor and a rational theologian, who used French androïde pejoratively, debunking [[see:Albertus Magnus]]'s talking head, giving [[gave:android]].
Albert the Great, said in legend to have made a talking bronze human or head offering advice; Naudé's description of it gave [[gave:android]].
Suffix meaning shaped like the thing before it, as in [[see:android]], [[see:humanoid]] and [[see:asteroid]]; a good sci-fi-sounding ending.
Human-shaped, which can apply to beings that aren't human; formed with [[from:-oid]].
Means star-shaped, though asteroids ultimately aren't; formed with [[from:-oid]].
Coined by [[see:Richard Dawkins]] in 1976 for a unit of cultural transmission, abbreviated from Greek [[from:mimeme]] to sound like [[see:gene]]; internet sense from 1998.
Coiner of [[see:meme]], who called gods ancient memes; author of The God Delusion, he attracts hate from both sides of the religious spectrum.
Dawkins wanted a monosyllable that sounded like gene, since [[see:meme]]s replicate like genes.
Comes from the same Greek root as [[same-root:meme]].
Comes from the same Greek root as [[same-root:meme]].
Dawkins said [[see:meme]] could be thought of as related to memory, though it isn't.
Dawkins said [[see:meme]] could be thought of as related to this French word, though it isn't.
Field arising from Dawkins's book, analogous to genetics, seeking to explain how ideas propagate; derived from [[from:meme]].
A 1998 quotation about a dancing baby animation; early uses of [[see:meme]] specified net or web because memes weren't yet exclusively online.
The fuller form people would now use instead of [[see:net meme]].
Short for the internet, more common decades ago (on the net), now passé like [[see:cyber]]; a brand using it would seem fussy.
The meat's name, from spiced ham, was suggested by [[see:Kenneth Daigneau]]; the junk-message sense refers to the [[from:Monty Python spam sketch]].
Sketch set in a [[see:greasy spoon]] full of Vikings chanting spam, drowning out everything, the source of email [[see:spam]].
British term for a cheap English cafe, like the setting of the [[see:Monty Python spam sketch]].
New York actor who won $100 in Hormel's competition for suggesting the name [[see:spam]] for its spiced ham.
Online discussion groups where the first [[see:spam]] is often said to have appeared, and the source of [[see:troll]].
Software developer who on 31 March 1993 accidentally sent a message 200 times to a [[see:Usenet]] group, often called the first [[see:spam]].
Predicted in 2004 that [[see:spam]] would be eradicated within two years.
Low-quality mass-produced AI output, with the same energy as [[see:spam]]; slop captures worthlessness and dirtiness, spawning portmanteaus like [[gave:slopaganda]].
AI optimism, usually used mockingly; a portmanteau from [[from:AI slop]].
A recent portmanteau spawned by [[from:AI slop]].
A recent portmanteau spawned by [[from:AI slop]].
A portmanteau from [[from:AI slop]] the hosts find beautiful, coined within the last 18 months or so.
From a 1992 [[see:Usenet]] user called Troll who incited arguments, evoking both [[see:trolling]] ships and a [[see:bridge troll]]; now any bad-faith online behaviour.
As a ship trolls, one image behind the internet [[see:troll]].
The other image behind the internet [[see:troll]].
Not related to [[unrelated:troll]].
Online harassment resulting in aggressive behaviour, the subject of the [[see:Usenet]] group where [[see:troll]] posted about flames and counterflames.
Sense of beyond or transcending comes from a misreading of [[from:Ta meta ta physika]]; Greek meta meant after, between or in the midst of.
His works were arranged by Greek scholars into collections including the [[see:Physics]] and [[see:Ta meta ta physika]].
The collection of [[see:Aristotle]]'s works on natural science, which [[see:Ta meta ta physika]] came after.
Field named after the collection [[from:Ta meta ta physika]], misread by Latin scholars as the science of what is beyond the physical.

entries.translation: that which comes after the physics
entries.note: Title of Aristotle's collection referring to its sequence after the [[see:Physics]], not its contents; misreading it [[gave:meta]] its sense of beyond.
Uses [[from:meta]] in its misunderstood sense of beyond.
Uses [[from:meta]] in its misunderstood sense of beyond.
Once seemed the imminent future, then felt dated after ChatGPT; Facebook renamed itself [[gave:Meta (company)]] for it; built with [[from:meta]] and [[from:-verse]].
Facebook's new name, adopted out of dedication to the [[from:metaverse]] and to own the term.
Made of Latin elements meaning turned into one; source of the back-formation [[gave:-verse]].
Back-formation from [[from:universe]], literally turn, now meaning world or realm; first used this way in [[see:Enderverse]], though [[see:multiverse]] is older; often a rebracketing.
A fictional universe named with [[from:-verse]].
A fictional universe named with [[from:-verse]].
A fictional universe named with [[from:-verse]].
[[see:Orson Scott Card]]'s name for the Ender's Game universe, cited as the first use of [[from:-verse]] in this way.
Coined [[see:Enderverse]] for his Ender's Game universe.
Coined by philosopher [[see:William James]] in the 1890s, showing the world sense of [[see:-verse]] is older than claimed.
Philosopher who coined [[see:multiverse]] in the 1890s.
Described as a space opera, a western cowboy wizard space story, whose words inspired by old languages make its world seem ancient.
Possibly from a Hebrew word, though the character was originally Minch Yoda; [[see:George Lucas]] wanted an eastern-sounding name for a Dalai Lama-like figure.
Creator of Star Wars, who explained choosing [[see:Yoda]] and named [[see:Darth Vader]] before planning him as Luke's father.
From Japanese [[from:jidaigeki]]; Lucas's first Jedi, the Jedi-Bendu, were based on [[see:samurai]], protectors of the emperor.
The model for Lucas's original [[see:Jedi]].
A Japanese genre meaning period drama, which [[gave:Jedi]].
Seems to mean dark father, [[see:vader]] being Dutch for father, but reportedly follows invader, as Darth Sidious follows insidious; Lucas hadn't planned the paternity.
Dutch for father, making [[see:Darth Vader]] a spoiler for Germanic speakers.
Named after insidious, mirroring [[see:Darth Vader]] from invader.
Not used for zapping until [[see:Buck Rogers in the 25th Century]] illustrated it as onomatopoeia; popularised as a ray-gun sound in sci-fi comics, now a verb.
The comic where [[see:zap]] was first used as an illustrated onomatopoeia.
Creator of Wash Tubs in the 1920s, credited as one of the first cartoonists to letter bold sound effects into panels, paving the way for [[see:zap]].
Stands for Tom A. Swift's Electric Rifle, a fictional weapon of [[see:Tom Swift]]; discussed more fully in an earlier episode.
Fictional character who debuted in novels in 1910, wielder of the rifle behind [[see:taser]] and inspiration for [[see:Tom Swifty]].
A quoted sentence whose attribution makes a pun, as in "We're out of flowers," said Tom lackadaisically; a recurring trope of the [[see:Tom Swift]] books.
